pages.text: The diode, the electric switch, the potentiometer and the transformer are $(item)bridges$().

Each one takes power in on one side (the $(item)back$() for the diode, switch and potentiometer) and feeds a $(item)separate network$() on its output side.$(br)The large switch and the large transformer work the same way across their two halves.

$(li)The input network sees the bridge as one consumer that uses what the output network uses.$(li)The output network gets its voltage from the bridge, and at most $(item)10 kW$() of power from the small bridges and the large switch. The large transformer passes more.
$(li)Small bridges burn above $(item)100 A$() and above the usual 1,000 V.$(li)If the input network runs short of power, the output one stops too.

$(l)Never close a loop$()$(br)If a chain of bridges feeds power back into a network it comes from, the bridge you just placed is $(item)destroyed without dropping$(). Always keep power flowing one way, from generators towards machines.
Splitting a factory into several networks lets you switch whole sections off and keeps one hungry machine from stalling everything.
